blocks.instruction: Leia o texto e escolha a alternativa correta. Algumas perguntas pedem inferência — a resposta não está escrita com todas as letras.
blocks.passage:
Interviewing a senior executive has remarkably little in common with interviewing a junior candidate. At the top of the organisation, almost every candidate already has the technical credentials. The real challenge is diagnostic: can you, in ninety minutes, form a credible view of how this person thinks, leads and makes difficult decisions under pressure?

The best executive interviewers resist the temptation of the polished narrative. They probe repeatedly. They ask about failures as rigorously as successes, paying close attention to the question behind the answer — the pattern of thinking, not the specific episode. If a candidate had handled their last transformation differently, what would have changed? What do they now wish they had done sooner?

The interview is also a two-way assessment. Senior candidates are interviewing the company at the same time. They watch how decisions are made in the process itself, how consistent the messages are across stakeholders, and whether the interviewers ask anything beyond surface-level questions. A weak process is one of the most visible signals a company can send.

items.q: According to the text, why is interviewing a senior executive mainly a diagnostic challenge?
options: Because technical skills are impossible to verify
Because senior candidates rarely tell the truth
Because ninety minutes is never enough time
Because most candidates already have the technical credentials
items.why: "almost every candidate already has the technical credentials. The real challenge is diagnostic".

items.q: How do the best interviewers treat a candidate's failures?
options: They avoid them to keep the tone positive
They examine them as rigorously as successes
They treat them as automatic disqualifiers
They leave them to a second interview
items.why: "They ask about failures as rigorously as successes".

items.q: What does the text say senior candidates do during the process?
options: They rehearse polished narratives in advance
They defer entirely to the interviewers
They negotiate compensation before anything else
They interview the company at the same time
items.why: "Senior candidates are interviewing the company at the same time."

items.q: The author would most likely DISAGREE with which statement?
options: The pattern of thinking matters more than the specific episode
A weak process can cost a company its best candidates
A confident, well-rehearsed story is the strongest sign of a good executive
Failures reveal as much as successes
items.why: Inferência: o texto adverte contra 'the polished narrative' e valoriza o padrão de raciocínio, não a história bem-ensaiada.

items.q: The phrase "the question behind the answer" suggests that the interviewer should focus on…
options: how the candidate reasons, beyond the surface story
the exact facts of the episode described
the length and polish of the candidate's reply
whether the candidate answers quickly
items.why: Inferência: 'the pattern of thinking, not the specific episode' — o interesse é no raciocínio, não no relato literal.

blocks.instruction: Ouça Oliver conduzindo uma entrevista executiva. Responda sem ler a transcrição — ela só aparece depois de corrigir.

audio.text:
Thank you for walking me through the turnaround. It reads well on paper, and I have no doubt the numbers recovered. But I'd like to stay with it a little longer, if you don't mind, because the story is a bit too clean for me.

You told me the plant was profitable again within eighteen months. What I'm more interested in is the first ninety days, when it clearly wasn't. Take me back there. Who did you disagree with, and what did you get wrong before you got it right?

Here's what I'm really asking. If you were dropped into that same situation tomorrow, knowing what you know now, what would you do differently in the first fortnight? And if you had made that call back then, what would have changed by the end of the year?

I ask because I don't need to hear that everything worked. Everyone's CV says that. I want to understand how you think when the plan is falling apart and the board is losing its nerve. That's the job, frankly — not the version we put in the annual report.
audio.label: Ouça quantas vezes precisar. A transcrição aparece depois de corrigir.

items.q: Why does Oliver want to "stay with it a little longer"?
options: Because he doubts the numbers ever recovered
Because the story feels a bit too clean to him
Because he is running short of time
Because the candidate refused to answer
items.why: "the story is a bit too clean for me."

items.q: Which period of the turnaround does Oliver most want to explore?
options: The eighteen months when it became profitable
The first ninety days, when it clearly wasn't working
The board meetings after the recovery
The candidate's very first week at the company
items.why: "What I'm more interested in is the first ninety days, when it clearly wasn't."

items.q: What does Oliver ask the candidate to imagine?
options: Interviewing for a more senior role
Presenting the results to the annual report
Managing a completely different plant abroad
Being dropped into the same situation tomorrow, knowing what they know now
items.why: "If you were dropped into that same situation tomorrow, knowing what you know now, what would you do differently".

items.q: What does Oliver imply when he says "Everyone's CV says that"?
options: That the candidate should submit a new CV
That claims of total success are unremarkable and unrevealing
That written CVs are more reliable than interviews
That the candidate copied another CV
items.why: Inferência: sucessos garantidos não distinguem ninguém; ele quer o que os currículos não mostram.

items.q: What is Oliver ultimately trying to assess?
options: How quickly the candidate can answer any question
Whether the candidate has enough years of experience
How the candidate thinks when the plan is falling apart
Whether the candidate can recite the annual report
items.why: Inferência: 'how you think when the plan is falling apart… That's the job' — ele avalia o julgamento sob pressão, não o relato polido.

blocks.instruction: O vocabulário da lição aparece aqui em frases novas. Escolha o sentido ou a palavra que cabe no contexto.

items.q: "The interview should be diagnostic, not confirmatory." Here diagnostic means the interview should…
options: focus on medical fitness for the role
confirm what the CV already claims
stay strictly within the allotted time
work out how the person actually thinks and leads
items.why: Diagnostic = diagnóstico: apurar como a pessoa pensa e decide, em vez de só confirmar.

items.q: Choose the correct word: "Instead of accepting the tidy account, she kept ___ until she understood the reasoning."
options: probing
delegating
drafting
signing
items.why: To probe = aprofundar, sondar; ela continuou sondando até entender o raciocínio.

items.q: "He offered a polished narrative, but avoided every hard question." A narrative here is…
options: a constructed story of events
an organisational chart
a financial statement
a formal contract
items.why: Narrative = narrativa: a história montada dos acontecimentos.

items.q: Choose the correct term: "The messages must stay consistent across every ___ , or candidates sense the organisation is divided."
options: credential
stakeholder
red flag
narrative
items.why: Stakeholder = parte interessada; a consistência da mensagem entre elas sinaliza maturidade.

items.q: "An interviewer who never goes past surface-level questions learns very little." Surface-level means…
options: hostile and aggressive
superficial, not going deep
carefully rehearsed
highly technical
items.why: Surface level = nível superficial: perguntas que não vão a fundo.

blocks.instruction: Expressões que aparecem em entrevistas e processos de seleção executivos. Escolha o sentido no contexto.

items.q: "The candidate's evasiveness on ethics was a real red flag." A red flag is…
options: a routine reference check
a formal offer of employment
a warning sign of a possible problem
a mark of outstanding performance
items.why: Red flag = sinal de alerta, algo que acende o alerta.

items.q: "Let's not gloss over the year the project failed." To gloss over means to…
options: examine in great detail
treat something too briefly to hide its problems
praise excessively
postpone to a later meeting
items.why: Gloss over = passar por cima, tratar de leve para esconder o problema.

items.q: "We need to dig into how she handled the board's panic." To dig into something means to…
options: leave it to HR
mention it in passing
approve it quickly
investigate it thoroughly
items.why: Dig into = aprofundar-se, investigar a fundo.

items.q: "When pressed, the candidate started to backpedal on his earlier claim." To backpedal on means to…
options: restate it more firmly
walk back or soften a previous position
write it down formally
delegate it to someone else
items.why: Backpedal on = recuar, amenizar uma posição assumida antes.

items.q: "A sloppy process will put off the very people you most want to hire." To put off means to…
options: delay a decision
formally reject
attract and impress
discourage or deter
items.why: Put off = afastar, desestimular; um processo ruim afugenta os melhores candidatos.
